## THE CURRENT MAP
21:18/q01 What does bal turn away from? [بَلْ · links] (turns on: Whether the contrast is read chiefly against the preceding talk of play or the opponents' claims about God.)
  21:18/q01/p1 It rejects the thought that God creates or acts in play, presenting His serious action against falsehood. — reasons: Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Ibn Ashur relate it to the preceding denial of amusement; Kashshaf and Razi invoke divine wisdom and self-sufficiency. Tabataba'i objects that a narrow contrast of earnestness and divine amusement would presuppose the amusement just denied.
  21:18/q01/p2 It dismisses the opponents' false claim that God has a child or partner. — reasons: Muqatil sets it against the Najran Christians' claim about Jesus and recalls that God would take a child from angels were He to do so; Wahidi connects it to their description of God, Bagawi and Ibn al-Jawzi call their statement a lie, and Jishumi links the alleged amusement to attribution of child and partner.
21:18/q02 What does naqdhif convey? [نَقْذِفُ · meaning]
  21:18/q02/p1 It means throwing or hurling truth forcefully against falsehood. — reasons: Wahidi and Bagawi give the basic sense; Raghib as cited by Bursevi and Alusi specifies a distant, forceful throw with hard impact. Tabataba'i also gives distance. Ibn Ashur extends the metaphor to proof, warning, destruction, a created force, discernment or empowerment of servants against wrongdoers (8:12).
21:18/q03 What are the truth and falsehood cast against each other? [بِٱلْحَقِّ ٱلْبَٰطِلِ · referent] (turns on: The notes variously identify the pair with revelation and lies, proof and claims, faith and shirk, seriousness and play, or unrestricted truth and falsehood.)
  21:18/q03/p1 The truth includes the Quran or God's revelation, and falsehood includes unbelievers' lies, denial or confusion. — reasons: Yahya, Tabari, Zajjaj, Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Biqai and Durr identify Quran or Book; Tabari specifies revelation against denial, Wahidi reports Abu Ishaq's Quran against lies, and Durr cites Qatada's confusion. Biqai stresses the Quran's firm argument and lack of frivolity.
  21:18/q03/p2 Truth is broad, including Quran, message, law, faith and all truth; falsehood covers their opposites generally. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya names Quran, message and law; Abu Hayyan reports the same broad view; Bagawi calls truth faith; Tabataba'i takes the rule across belief, practice and creation; Alusi prefers the general reading over restriction to proof and claims about a child. Bursevi includes seriousness, faith and Quran.
  21:18/q03/p3 Truth is Quran and falsehood is Satan or Iblis. — reasons: Tabari reports Qatada; Mawardi reports the alternative; Abu Hayyan reports Mujahid, who says every Quranic use of falsehood means Satan; Alusi also reports Mujahid. Nasafi lists Satan among possible referents.
  21:18/q03/p4 Truth is proof or decisive argument, and falsehood is the opponents' claims, doubt or false descriptions of God. — reasons: Nahhas identifies proofs and arguments against their claim; Tabrisi gives decisive proofs, with argument against doubt as a variant; Abu Hayyan and Alusi mention the claim of a child; Jishumi says proofs distinguish truth from falsehood; Wahidi says truth exposes lies.
  21:18/q03/p5 Truth is God's word that He has no child; falsehood is their claim that He took one. — reasons: Bagawi explicitly offers this alternative; Muqatil applies the clash to the Najran claim about Jesus.
  21:18/q03/p6 Truth is Islam or faith, and falsehood is polytheism or disbelief. — reasons: Mawardi gives Islam against polytheism; Tabrisi gives faith against disbelief; Nasafi gives Islam against idolatry; Yahya identifies falsehood as shirk.
  21:18/q03/p7 Truth is the word to be followed, and falsehood the word to be rejected. — reasons: Mawardi reports this formulation without a named transmitter.
  21:18/q03/p8 Truth is earnestness and falsehood is play or amusement. — reasons: Nasafi lists it; Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi use the seriousness/play contrast. Tabataba'i reports and rejects a reading that assumes God was amusing Himself.
  21:18/q03/p9 Truth is God's transcendence, and falsehood is treating Him as immanent in or coexistent with creation. — reasons: Asad argues that finite, perishable creation cannot be a projection of the infinite, eternal Creator.
21:18/q04 What does yadmughuhu mean? [فَيَدْمَغُهُۥ · meaning]
  21:18/q04/p1 It strikes the head or brain, a fatal blow, and thus destroys or defeats falsehood. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba, Tabari, Mawardi, Wahidi citing Ibn Qutayba, Bagawi, Ibn Atiyya, Samīn, Jishumi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Baydawi, Tabataba'i, Islahi and Study Quran cite the brain wound; Samīn compares verbs named for the struck body part. Study Quran adds the usage of stamping a form into soft material. Ibn Ashur and Alusi describe breaking a hollow object; Kalbi gives destruction and Tabrisi invalidation.
21:18/q05 How does the casting and crushing image work? [نَقْذِفُ فَيَدْمَغُهُۥ · rhetoric] (turns on: Alusi's distinction is between an explicit overall simile and a concealed comparison through the physical verbs.)
  21:18/q05/p1 It depicts strong truth as a hard projectile crushing weak, hollow falsehood, making abstract defeat vivid. — reasons: Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai and Bursevi give the hard/soft image; Bursevi cites Sahib al-Miftah on physical words transferred to abstract realities; Burhan says both verbs are metaphors. Alusi prefers a full simile of thrown body and soft brain, with truth's height and falsehood's lowliness, to a hidden metaphor. Ibn Ashur says both images transfer physical action to thought. Abu Ishaq, cited by Wahidi, says the defeat makes falsehood disappear in abasement and humiliation.
  21:18/q05/p2 The image may be a hidden metaphor comparing truth and falsehood to the two bodies. — reasons: Alusi states this alternative but prefers the full simile.
21:18/q06 How is fa-yadmaghuhu read and parsed? [فَيَدْمَغُهُۥ · readings] (turns on: The final verb's case or mood and the possible source of the rare mim vowel.)
  21:18/q06/p1 The common reading raises the final ghayn, coordinating the imperfect verb. — reasons: Samīn calls this the common reading and its grammatical coordination; Sibawayh notes more generally that jussive inflection belongs to imperfect verbs and compares it to noun genitive.
  21:18/q06/p2 Isa ibn Umar reads the final ghayn with accusative/subjunctive inflection. — reasons: Kashshaf calls it weak and cites a poetic subjunctive ending fa-astariha; Abu Hayyan and Samīn repeat that judgment. Baydawi parses by meaning or coordination with al-haqq and cites anonymous poetry. Alusi says fa does not govern it here; Abu al-Baqa coordinates it with al-haqq, while Alusi prefers coordination with the underlying sense of throwing then crushing. A proposed indicative with light emphatic nun in the poem is weak, making the verse reading weaker.
  21:18/q06/p3 A rare reading puts a damma on the mim, and another transmits damma on mim and ghayn. — reasons: Abu Hayyan transmits the mim variant from Zamakhshari; Samīn explains it as dialect variation in the imperfect or assimilation from the guttural; Alusi reports both vowels raised.
21:18/q07 What does zahiq mean? [زَاهِقٌۭ · meaning] (turns on: Jishumi lists a separate lexical usage, while the contextual glosses agree on disappearance.)
  21:18/q07/p1 It is departing, vanishing or perishing. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba, Zajjaj, linguists cited by Nahhas, Qatada cited by Abd al-Razzaq, Tabari, Mawardi, Wahidi and Tabrisi, and later commentators give these near senses. Ibn Abbas compares departure to an arrow leaving its target; Baydawi and Ibn Ashur recall the departing soul. Ibn Ashur cites 9:55 and 17:81; Study Quran cites Tabari's gloss of destruction.
  21:18/q07/p2 In another Arabic usage, zahiq describes a fat or stout animal. — reasons: Jishumi lists this beside perishing and the usage 'his soul departed'; he does not claim the animal sense is intended here.
21:18/q08 What does fa-idha huwa zahiq add? [فَإِذَا هُوَ زَاهِقٌۭ · rhetoric]
  21:18/q08/p1 The sudden particle and nominal clause make falsehood's complete disappearance seem immediate and startling. — reasons: Bursevi and Alusi identify the suddenness and nominal sentence; Alusi says as though it never existed. Ibn Ashur says clear truth works swiftly and compares 13:17. Tabataba'i sees a surprising reversal; Islahi likens it to immediate death from a brain blow.
21:18/q09 What does wayl mean here? [ٱلْوَيْلُ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the valley is the intended referent or merely a way to express deserved punishment.)
  21:18/q09/p1 It denotes woe, ruin, evil, reproach, grief or distress. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba calls it comprehensive evil and quotes Asma'i on condemnation; Itqan repeats Asma'i and cites laments at 18:49 and 5:31. Ibn Atiyya gives disgrace and grief; Bursevi cites Asma'i on ugliness and lament, distinguishes ways as belittling and wayh as compassion. Ibn Qutayba notes diminutive wayh and ways and a separate Arabic word al-alil for groaning; Itqan cites Aisha's report that the Prophet treated wayh/ways as mercy but warned of wayl.
  21:18/q09/p2 It may designate a valley in Hell. — reasons: Wahidi reports Ibn Abbas; Ibn Atiyya allows this as an intended sense if the view is adopted. Bursevi says those calling it a valley mean the condemned have an abode in the Fire, not that the valley is its lexical meaning.
21:18/q10 How does lakum function with al-wayl? [وَلَكُمُ ٱلْوَيْلُ · grammar]
  21:18/q10/p1 The lam has its ordinary genitive form in lakum al-wayl. — reasons: Sibawayh contrasts it with the open lam of vocative ya wayla laka: without ya the lam returns to its normal form.
21:18/q11 How is mimma tasifun construed? [مِمَّا تَصِفُونَ · grammar] (turns on: The attachment of the prepositional phrase and whether ma names the act
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<21:18 update 1, part 1 of 0..2>>
 of describing or the object described.)
  21:18/q11/p1 It attaches to an implied state or predicate: woe is fixed for you because of your descriptions. — reasons: Samīn prefers implied istiqrar and causal min; Alusi lists causal and descriptive possibilities, including that ruin arises from the descriptions.
  21:18/q11/p2 It is circumstantial, qualifying the woe that comes upon them because of their descriptions. — reasons: Samīn reports Abu al-Baqa's parsing.
  21:18/q11/p3 Ma may be a verbal noun, a relative pronoun, or an indefinite relative/adjective. — reasons: Samīn says the verbal noun needs no resumptive pronoun, whereas relative readings require an omitted one under appropriate conditions; Alusi gives causal 'what you describe,' describable things, or ruin produced by description.
21:18/q12 Who receives the closing address and threat? [وَلَكُمُ ٱلْوَيْلُ · referent] (turns on: Whether direct address continues the present opponents or shifts to another group in the surrounding narrative.)
  21:18/q12/p1 It addresses the unbelievers or polytheists being argued against, especially Quraysh or Arab unbelievers. — reasons: Alusi explicitly identifies Quraysh or all Arab unbelievers and says they face the fate of earlier communities; he says the direct address plainly returns to those just mentioned. Tabari, Bagawi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and others locate the threat among opponents describing God falsely.
  21:18/q12/p2 The address turns to those denying the messengers and calling the Quran magic or confused dreams. — reasons: Razi gives this audience; Abu Hayyan reports it but calls the proposed shift from third person to direct address remote. Ibn Ashur connects it to allegations against Muhammad and the Quran in 21:3 and 21:5.
  21:18/q12/p3 The address shifts to the former inhabitants of ruined towns. — reasons: Alusi reports and rejects this as far-fetched because it relies on their earlier plea.
21:18/q13 What descriptions bring woe? [مِمَّا تَصِفُونَ · referent] (turns on: The referent of 'what you describe' in the immediate argument: divine attributes, lies and shirk, accusations about revelation, or other beliefs.)
  21:18/q13/p1 Attributing to God a child, spouse, partner or other unfitting qualities. — reasons: Qatada specifies angels called daughters; Muqatil specifies Jesus as son; Tabari includes wife and child and says lies and shirk both fit, while nearest wording favors this reading. Zajjaj, Wahidi citing Abu Ishaq, Bagawi, Tabrisi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi and Alusi agree on false divine attributes.
  21:18/q13/p2 Their lies generally, including untrue descriptions of God. — reasons: Tabari cites Qatada on lies; Wahidi cites Mujahid with 6:139; Bagawi repeats Mujahid; Durr cites Hasan that every liar is liable. Study Quran lists lies as one reading; Tabari says lying and shirk can both fit.
  21:18/q13/p3 Their idolatry and attribution of partners to God. — reasons: Tabari cites Ibn Jurayj and his comparison with 21:22 and Mujahid on 6:139; Study Quran cites 7:190, 23:92 and 27:63.
  21:18/q13/p4 Their accusations about the Prophet or Quran, such as magic and confused dreams. — reasons: Razi and Abu Hayyan mention rejection of the Messenger; Ibn Ashur links allegations to 21:3 and 21:5. Study Quran reports a reading tied to 21:3–5; Bursevi includes these accusations as well as claims about God.
  21:18/q13/p5 Their claim that the world is sport and that polytheistic intercessors will save them. — reasons: Islahi says idolaters expected their deities to rescue them in the hereafter and therefore felt no fear.
  21:18/q13/p6 Defining God as immanent in creation. — reasons: Asad says describing also means defining Him; he cites 6:100 and argues such definition of God's Being is erroneous.
21:18/q14 How widely does the warning apply? [وَلَكُمُ ٱلْوَيْلُ مِمَّا تَصِفُونَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the specific address also states a standing rule for later false descriptions.)
  21:18/q14/p1 It extends to anyone making a false description until the Resurrection, including false claims about God's attributes or rulings. — reasons: Wahidi reports Hasan and applies it to attributes and rulings; Durr reports Hasan; Biqai extends it to descriptions of Quran, God and world made on whim without divine warrant because people lack full grasp of realities.
  21:18/q14/p2 The warning specifically condemns the contemporary unbelievers' false assertions. — reasons: Wahidi and Bagawi describe their unfitting attribution; Alusi identifies the immediate addressees; Tabataba'i identifies deniers of resurrection and prophethood.
21:18/q15 What lasting relation between truth and falsehood does the verse teach? [* · theology] (turns on: The notes distinguish an unrestricted metaphysical rule from the specific means of its enactment.)
  21:18/q15/p1 Truth has real stability and ultimately overcomes transient falsehood throughout belief, practice and creation. — reasons: Tabataba'i says falsehood only resembles truth, like mirage water; its deficiencies depend on a more complete reality and it exists by God's permission. He invokes 13:17, 24:25, 2:147 and 38:27, calls God absolute truth, and says the imperfect verb signals God's continuing practice. Kuranyolu says falsehood cannot remain in truth's presence; the Sadiq reports generalize the rule. Study Quran points to 17:81, 8:8, 34:49 and 42:24.
  21:18/q15/p2 God's truth overcomes falsehood through revealed proof, warning, destruction, discernment or force against wrongdoers. — reasons: Ibn Ashur enumerates these means and cites 8:12; Tabrisi says God who manifests truth by proofs cannot play falsehood; Ibn Kathir says He makes truth plain and erases falsehood.
21:18/q16 Why is falsehood given time before truth defeats it? [* · theology]
  21:18/q16/p1 Respite tests human choice and does not put good and evil on equal footing; God then makes truth prevail. — reasons: Islahi states the trial of those choosing truth or clinging to evil; Tabataba'i says God gives falsehood time but preserves true belief, perfection and prophetic victory despite few followers or strong opposition.
21:18/q17 What does the verse imply about human knowledge and freedom? [* · theology] (turns on: These are two distinct doctrinal implications drawn by Jishumi, rather than rival readings.)
  21:18/q17/p1 It refutes necessary knowledge, since universal compulsion to know would leave no disagreement. — reasons: Jishumi argues that if knowledge were necessary everyone would form one community.
  21:18/q17/p2 It refutes determinism, since sending prophets presupposes that people can move from unbelief to faith. — reasons: Jishumi draws this conclusion from prophetic missions.
21:18/q18 Must every era contain someone who speaks the truth? [* · theology] (turns on: Whether the verse itself establishes continuous witnesses or that continuity requires separate transmitted proof.)
  21:18/q18/p1 Yes: each era has some witnesses for truth, even if few. — reasons: Abu Ali reads broad wording as allowing this despite predominating unbelief. The Qadi says the argument works only if the existence of such a person in every era is established, which it has not been.
  21:18/q18/p2 The verse permits an era with no truth-speaker, though transmitted Islamic law rules that out. — reasons: Jishumi says consensus is transmitted proof that no era lacks affirmers of truth; the verse alone permits all people to be unbelievers.
21:18/q19 How does the verse connect to other passages and the sura's argument? [* · links] (turns on: The connections differ by neighboring argument versus verbal and thematic parallels elsewhere.)
  21:18/q19/p1 It follows the denial of purposeless creation and supports the surrounding argument for God's wisdom and oneness. — reasons: Islahi says a wise, just Creator will bring a day when truth wins; multiple independent gods would undo the universe, all prophets taught monotheism, and angels are servants rather than daughters or autonomous intercessors. Jishumi links 21:7 on human messengers and creation by idols, and 21:17 on child and partner claims. Abu Muslim links good overcoming evil to 21:18.
  21:18/q19/p2 Other verses echo the disappearance of falsehood and the punishment of false description. — reasons: Wahidi compares 17:81 and Mujahid's gloss of 6:139; Tabari compares 21:22 and 6:139; Ibn Ashur cites 13:17, 9:55 and 17:81; Study Quran compares 17:81, 8:8, 34:49, 42:24 and the sura's close at 21:112.
21:18/q20 What reports apply the truth's victory more broadly? [* · reports]
  21:18/q20/p1 Al-Sadiq is reported to say truth defeats falsehood whenever they meet, and reaches every person. — reasons: Yunus transmits the first report through al-Mahasin; Ayyub ibn al-Hurr transmits the second, saying truth breaks the heart of one who accepts or leaves it. Tabataba'i says both generalize the verse.
21:18/q21 What inward readings are drawn from truth overcoming falsehood? [* · inward] (turns on: The degree of inward defeat: moral acts, attributes, or all created selfhood.)
  21:18/q21/p1 Admonition or divine command defeats sin and forbidden acts. — reasons: Sulami twice transmits Wasiti's admonition of spiritual elders; Mawardi reports contemplatives' admonitions against sins. Bursevi cites Najm al-Din's first level, divine commands against forbidden acts, with 28:88 and 17:81.
  21:18/q21/p2 Manifestation of divine attributes or Essence effaces servant attributes and created essences. — reasons: Bursevi cites Najm al-Din's second and third levels. He reports Maghribi's explanation of ana al-haqq as an ecstatic utterance after the speaker's false self vanishes in manifestation; Maghribi's verse calls the Real the servant's defender, and Khujandi's verses link the secret to self-annihilation at the gallows and a costly, lofty insight.
21:18/q22 What Fatiha and angel reports occur among these notes? [* · reports] (turns on: Whether the angel prayer anecdote pe

rmits angelic recitation or recitation remains a human privilege.)
  21:18/q22/p1 An anecdote suggests angels recite al-Fatiha alone. — reasons: A man saw Umar pray at night with only al-Fatiha, then glorify, bow and prostrate; Umar called it the angels' prayer. Suyuti infers that angels were permitted to recite al-Fatiha alone.
  21:18/q22/p2 Quran recitation is a human privilege, while angels long to hear it. — reasons: Suyuti reports Ibn al-Salah's view.
21:18/q23 What merits are reported for hearing or reciting al-Fatiha? [* · reports] (turns on: These reports describe different acts and rewards.)
  21:18/q23/p1 Hearing its opening or completion earns merit likened to witnessing battle or distribution of spoils. — reasons: Abu Qilaba transmits this from the Prophet.
  21:18/q23/p2 Reciting it with another sura before sleep brings an angel companion on waking. — reasons: Suyuti reports this Prophetic saying.
21:18/q24 What is reported about al-Fatiha in prayer? [* · law]
  21:18/q24/p1 Prayer without al-Fatiha is invalid or deficient; al-Fatiha can substitute for other recitation but nothing substitutes for it. — reasons: Suyuti reports the Prophet's 'no prayer' ruling, the Mother of the Quran's unique sufficiency, Abu Hurayra's deficient/deceptive prayer report, and a threefold repetition that prayer without the Mother of the Book is deficient.

## THE NEW NOTES
[RUMMANI:v1p88/r6] RUMMANI, d. 384 · author | holds | قذف is stronger than bringing truth to bear because it depicts truth as forcibly overpowering falsehood, leaving no room for doubt or hesitation.
[RUMMANI:v1p88/r7] RUMMANI, d. 384 · author | holds | يدمغه is stronger than يذهبه because it conveys an impact on falsehood, making the allusion clearer and the force greater.
[QASHANI:21:1/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | In one reading, demonstrative and unveiled certainty is hurled against false belief and crushes it, including denial of resurrection.
[QASHANI:21:1/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Alternatively, God's essential disclosure in the greater resurrection overcomes transient beings, revealing them as perishing and exposing claims of independent existence, attributes, acts, or effects as false.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p403#3/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | دمغه means striking the brain; by extension one says a person struck someone’s liver or head when hitting those organs.
[BURHAN:v3p442/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Both throwing and striking through the skull are borrowed expressions in the description of truth overcoming falsehood.
[BURHAN:v4p443/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Asma'i says ويل expresses condemnation, though it can also mark grief and lament.
[ITQAN:v3p121/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Qadhf and damgh are metaphors from perceptible action, while haqq and batil are abstract; the shared relation makes the borrowing intelligible.
